title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
description: Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.Last weekend, the DE civic ac
body: Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina. During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students. A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used."From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything." Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs. A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force. Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment. An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number."It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC."The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power. The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other. Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement. "There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC. "In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

schema.headline: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán

title: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
description: Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.Besides Frankfurt - Germany's f
body: Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.As night fell, demonstrations turned violent.A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed. The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing trainers and other items, local media reported.Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.Poseck said: "We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe. In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.Thousands of police officers were deployed across France to deal with the demonstrations, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.There were more than 500 arrests after clashes in Toulouse, Lyon and Marseille.French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail. Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

schema.headline: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent

title: What are the US midterms? A simple guide
description: ByJames FitzGeraldUpdated 26 October 2026There are just days to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a
body: ByJames FitzGeraldUpdated 26 October 2026There are just days to go until the US midterm elections, when voters take part in a ballot that could have a major impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.What are the midterms?On 3 November, Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.Who is being elected?All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. They serve fixed terms of two years. The House is commonly where proposed laws are introduced and debated.Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs. Senators serve six-year terms. Among other jobs, they approve or block proposed laws that have been received from the House.On the same day, voters across much of the US will also choose state-level politicians. Governor contests in California, Florida, Georgia and Michigan will be among the most closely watched.What are the key issues?The US economy is on the minds of many voters struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare.Inflation remains above the level targeted by the US Federal Reserve, partly down to the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.Democrats argue Trump's programme of trade tariffs has also pushed up prices for Americans.Immigration is another key issue. Republicans say Trump has delivered on a major campaign pledge in 2024 by tightening the border and launching a widespread - and often controversial - crackdown on illegal immigration.Concerns over AI have grown in urgency in recent weeks. Senior politicians from both parties have agreed on the need to regulate it - setting themselves in opposition to Trump, who has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology. What is at stake?Congress is one of the three branches of government, alongside the presidency and the judiciary. Control of it matters for the shaping of legislation.Both the House and Senate are currently held by the Republican Party. But its majority is a slender one. They have 218 seats in the House, which is the minimum number needed to control it, plus one independent who votes with them. In the Senate, they have 53 seats. The upper chamber will only change hands if the Democrats win 51 seats, which would overcome a tie-breaking vote by the vice-president - currently a Republican - in the event of both sides getting 50.If opposition Democrats win back control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor.Who might win?Voters have tended to "punish" the party of the president in the past and vote against them.Recent polling shows a low approval rating for the president. He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but in early October it was sitting at about 37%. Meanwhile 61% disapproved of him.But not all seats in each chamber are competitive. Some are a safe bet for Republicans or Democrats.The BBC's US partner CBS News has identified ten Senate races to watch, external, in states like Iowa and New Hampshire, and 42 House races, in states like Arizona and Ohio.The vote is more unpredictable this year because of a battle between the two parties over the way voting districts in the House of Representatives are drawn.Republicans tried to gain an advantage by creating more favourable electoral maps in certain states and Democrats followed suit.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Josh Turek (Democrat) and Ashley Hinson (Republican) are in a tight race for Iowa's Senate seatWhat does it mean for Trump?If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get any laws through Congress.So his domestic plans could be frustrated, although he has found ways to exercise power without his wider party.Democratic control of either chamber would also mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency. Corruption allegations, the new White House ballroom and ICE tactics could be subject to scrutiny.There is also a debate within the Democratic Party about whether to impeach Trump, which means to bring charges in Congress that will form the basis for a political, not criminal, trial.If the Republican Party stays in control of Congress, Trump will be able to keep going with his plans for the remainder of his time in office.What does it mean for the 2028 election?The president's name is not on the ballot during the midterm elections, though Trump has urged Republicans to pretend that it is by voting for him as an endorsement of his actions so far.Whichever way the results fall, commentators are likely to use them to make arguments about how voters feel about the direction of the country under Trump's leadership.Trump cannot run to be president a third time. After the midterms, we can expect speculation to start building about who might be his successor as the Republican presidential nominee for 2028 - and who might compete against that person for the Democrats.Additional reporting by Deirdre Finnerty

schema.headline: What are the US midterms? A simple guide

title: Ash Dykes completes Congo Basin expedition after going 'missing' for 24 hours
description: Adventurer completes 400-mile expedition after losing contact with teamImage source, Will PerezImage caption, Ash Dykes' latest challenge involves six
body: Adventurer completes 400-mile expedition after losing contact with teamImage source, Will PerezImage caption, Ash Dykes' latest challenge involves six back-to-back feats of extreme enduranceByMatthew RichardsBBC WalesAn adventurer has completed the first leg of his latest challenge after losing contact with his UK team for almost 24 hours.Ash Dykes, 35, from Old Colwyn, Conwy, holds five world records but his most recent quest was the first of six back-to-back expeditions he will take on in extreme environments.Dykes encountered elephants, gorillas and was chased by "killer" bees as he rowed more than 434 miles (700 km) along rivers in the Congo Basin, central Africa. Towards the end of the journey, Dykes' portable satellite kit lost power. He said: "My parents and fiancée were worrying but as soon as I had a bit of signal I made sure I got in touch".Figure caption, Ash says the world is not ready for a "truly live expedition"In his latest Project 6 challenge, Dykes will attempt six expeditions in very different locations.He has previously walked 4,000-miles (6,437km) along the length of China's Yangtze River in 2019 and kayaked the length of the Coppename river in Suriname from source to sea in 37 daysOn "going missing", Dykes said his "power bank just shut down"."We were underneath the jungle canopy, because we were staying with a small community, and then it took me about 20 hours before I could get out the first message," he said. As the adventurer is sharing expeditions "live", he said he had learned lessons from the experience going forward. He said: "I don't think the world's ready for a truly live expedition so I've learned from that..."If I lose contact again with the team, we have to keep it within the team because I do know that that hit alarms and a lot of people were stressed and panicked. So it's important to make this as live as possible, but moving forward, it can't be that live anymore."Image source, Will PerezImage caption, Ash Dykes was joined by local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire and videographer Will PerezDuring the adventure, Dykes said his biggest fear was not the danger posed by wildlife or disease, but the extreme heat during many hours of kayaking in rivers home to crocodiles and hippos with no shade.He said: "We took the warnings seriously. Experience means listening to local advice, reading the conditions and making the decisions that get your team through safely."For the explorer, the main highlight was spending time with the Baka tribe, a semi-nomadic indigenous ethnic group.They demonstrated their hunting prowess which involves trapping animals in netting set up around the jungle."They were amazing, they took us under their wings, they showed us how they survive, how they hunt, how they gather," Dykes said. "They took us to an area where we saw a group of gorillas within Sanga National Park. I was about five metres away from silverback."Image source, Will PerezImage caption, Ash Dykes was waved off on his journey by local peopleDykes was joined on his trek by local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire as well as videographer Will Perez, who has been helping chart the journey with regular social media posts.His popularity on TikTok has soared following his latest adventure.Dykes said: "It felt like the world was on the river with us."But he added some followers were disappointed in the lack of drama."Everyone wanted that excitement, that danger, but if something was to happen, I'd be criticised: 'this is dangerous'."Now that I've made it unscathed, everyone's like: 'It's easy, there were no crocs'."So there's no true winning when you go that viral."He said he lost 11lbs (5kg) during the trip, as he was relying mostly on ration packs of food.In a social media post to mark the end of the first stage of Project 6, Dykes said: "It's been a lot. We've faced ups and downs - seen some crazy wildlife, but more importantly we've survived."Dykes said he would reveal the second stage of Project 6 next week, and hinted it would be somewhere "a lot colder" than the Congo Basin.

schema.headline: Ash Dykes completes Congo Basin expedition after going 'missing' for 24 hours

title: Stranded in the Cook Islands: Why I can't get home to Sri Lanka
description: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly homeImage source, SuppliedByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor a
body: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly homeImage source, SuppliedByAyeshea PereraAsia Digital Editor and Dinuk HewawitharanaBBC SinhalaWhen Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving."My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears."I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.It turned out to be a disastrous decision.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Cook Islands is known for its beaches and volcanic peaks - but Ruchira Ranasingha is an involuntary guestShe was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do"."She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected."I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.Image source, SuppliedOn a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income."My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says."I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried."Her mental state is not good," her tells BBC Sinhala."One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."Additional reporting by Kethaki Masilamani and Julianna KhanIf you've been affected by issues involving suicide or feelings of despair, details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line. Help and support outside the UK can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.

schema.headline: Stranded in the Cook Islands: Why I can't get home to Sri Lanka

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
description: The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty clean
body: The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins."We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal."It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area."I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".

schema.headline: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests

title: Lewis Hamilton enjoys Mexico City Grand Prix pole as Kimi Antonelli aims to clinch title
description: So far, Kimi Antonelli has been a wallflower at his own party at the Mexico City Grand Prix.Fourth place on the grid is low-key for the Mercedes drive
body: So far, Kimi Antonelli has been a wallflower at his own party at the Mexico City Grand Prix.Fourth place on the grid is low-key for the Mercedes driver in the context of his season as a whole - and the gargantuan achievement of which he stands on the brink.It still puts the 20-year-old Italian in a strong position to seal the maiden title that will make him the youngest champion in history.But on Saturday that was overshadowed by the veteran whose seat Antonelli took at Mercedes, as Lewis Hamilton secured his first pole position for Ferrari and his first for more than three years.The seven-time champion edged out his former Mercedes team-mate George Russell by just 0.009 seconds to clinch his first pole since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix and the 105th of his stellar career.Fittingly, the only two drivers who, at least mathematically, can prevent Antonelli from sealing the deal on Sunday are together on the front row.The only possible way in which Antonelli will not become champion at the end of the race is if either Hamilton or Russell win. Even then, he needs only to finish ninth if it's Russell or 10th if it's Hamilton to be sure.Hamilton said the idea was not even in his mind."That's not really something we're thinking of," he said. "We're thinking of just trying to score the best result for the team."Kimi, he's continued to drive really well and doing what he needs to do. All he has to do is just finish where he is, and he's kind of on his own journey."Our journey is to focus on performing the best we can this weekend and holding on to second in the Constructors' Championship."Russell said it was "obviously inevitable" that Antonelli would win the championship, adding that it would be "most likely this weekend".He continued: "So, for me personally, just going out there to try to have a good race. I want to try to finish this season strong. That's the biggest priority for me."In my mind, he's kind of already won the championship. So that's something that I don't think I need to deal with."Antonelli, though, would not agree with Hamilton's assessment of his weekend so far.He has looked quick at times, but in qualifying it did not come together, and he ended up 0.184secs off Russell. He was fifth fastest, but a one-place penalty for Red Bull's Max Verstappen puts Antonelli on the second row alongside Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc.Antonelli admitted that the high stakes of the weekend were on his mind, to the extent that it was affecting his driving."I just feel like I didn't do a good enough job out there and didn't have the most confidence," he said."It hasn't been easy this weekend, to be fair, and especially to keep my emotions flat. Definitely I have been a bit more tense than usual, also that played a big factor."But I try to enjoy the evening with family and friends and focus on tomorrow."Hamilton said his pole, on his 43rd start for Ferrari, was "one of the greatest feelings".It is not the first time he has qualified fastest for Ferrari - that was when he took sprint pole at the Chinese Grand Prix last year, in only his second race for the team.But that was followed by a difficult debut season, when he looked a shadow of his former self, and was pretty much taken to the cleaners by Leclerc.Hamilton's record is such that his performances last year left many perplexed - not least himself. He was consistently down on himself, even saying at one low point in the summer of 2025 that he was "just useless" and suggesting Ferrari should change drivers.As this followed a similarly challenging final year for Mercedes, it inevitably led to questions about his future, whether age was catching up with him. After all, he had no explanations for his performances himself.His form has improved this year, with a car that he finds much more to his liking, and he has a number of times referenced these perfectly valid questions. He did so again on Saturday."It's impossible to rank 105 pole positions," he said. "They have all been unique in their own way. It feels more special in this period where they're not every week and it's the first one with Ferrari in red."I've now had pole with three different teams, which is pretty phenomenal. And all the questions people had about whether a 40-year-old has still got it, there you go."The battle between Hamilton and Leclerc has been much more even this year.Hamilton leads his team-mate by eight points in the championship and in qualifying there is nothing to choose between them - it is now 12-10 in their head-to-head and Leclerc is ahead on average pace by just 0.037secs, when the gap was 0.15secs last year."I have been fortunate to have many great experiences with Mercedes over the years," said Hamilton. "We have had sprint pole but I have been really dreaming and eyeing for that first pole with the team."Charles is very, very quick over one lap. He has had an engineer he has worked with for years. It's an environment he is very aware of and used to."I am still settling in and learning, with new engineers this year. We have really found a good rapport and are really doing a great job. There is lots more to come, we just have to keep on at it, but what an amazing feeling to get that first."Hamilton goes into the race with less knowledge than his rivals, a breakdown in second practice meaning he was not able to do his race-simulation run."It will will be a massive challenge to find the right balance but I am hopeful, it will be challenging and tough," he said.For Antonelli, fourth is not such a bad place to start.For one thing, he does not need any heroics. As long as he brings it home, he will become champion and fulfil a lifetime's ambition, as well as smash the record for the youngest-ever title winner by more than three years.But jeopardy still exists.The run to the first corner in Mexico is long, more than 800m. Drivers on the second row have several times over the years used the slipstream to rocket into the lead.Leclerc will be trying to do that, and the temptation may also be there for Antonelli. But the last thing he needs is to become embroiled in a first-corner pile-up.The tension will doubtless still be there. But it's only a matter of time before it's released."Records are there to be broken, you know," said Hamilton, who described what Antonelli is achieving as "phenomenal". "He's just got such a bright future ahead of him," added Hamilton. "I'm grateful that I can be racing in the time to see it, to witness it."I do hope in the future we get to have some actual battles because we didn't get to have any battles this year. It just flew past us on all the straights, more often than not."So, I hope next year that we're able to give him a bit more of a fight and get it really down to race craft. And, yeah, I'll be so happy for him."

schema.headline: Lewis Hamilton enjoys Mexico City Grand Prix pole as Kimi Antonelli aims to clinch title

title: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash
description: A University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train disaster which killed at least 69 people, a research institute has confirmed.Dr Marta Sh
body: A University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train disaster which killed at least 69 people, a research institute has confirmed.Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling on one of the trains involved in the collision near Urda, south of Madrid, according to the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in the city, where she led a group of researchers. The University of Cambridge lists Dr Shahbazi as an affiliate associate professor. The Spanish CiMUS institute paid tribute to the "brilliant young researcher" in a social media post. The expert in cell biology, who runs the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, was announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development.She was due to be presented with the award during the society's conference in El Rompido, Andalusia, south-west Spain.The LMB previously confirmed Dr Shahbazi was on one of the trains but said her whereabouts were "unknown", external. In a social media post, external CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela said: "The CiMUS community would like to express its support and deepest sympathies to our dear PI María José Alonso, following the death of her niece, Marta Shahbazi, in the railway accident that occurred on 28 October."Marta was a brilliant young researcher, group leader at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology and Affiliate Associate Professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, University of Cambridge."The institute said Dr Shahbazi's aunt worked at their centre. Dr Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.The collision happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.More than 540 people were on board both trains.Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, said one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.

schema.headline: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash

title: Ferritin face: Can you really diagnose low iron from your looks?
description: "Do you have ferritin face?" a young woman asks on TikTok, pointing to dark circles, washed-out skin and brittle hair, alongside before-and-after styl
body: "Do you have ferritin face?" a young woman asks on TikTok, pointing to dark circles, washed-out skin and brittle hair, alongside before-and-after style photographs. The content creator puts these features down to her iron levels.It is one of a growing number of videos and posts on TikTok and Instagram claiming that low ferritin - a protein which stores iron in the body - can leave visible clues on your face.Users list pale or grey-looking skin, dark under-eye circles, dry or cracked lips, hair shedding and weak nails, while others share portraits claiming stark visual differences.The phrase "ferritin face" has spread widely across social media, with videos attracting millions of views.But doctors say appearance alone cannot diagnose iron deficiency."Ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis," said GP Dr Aziza Sesay, who is based in the West Midlands. "However, it may be a clue to tell us that something is going on."Pale skin, hair shedding or brittle nails can accompany low iron, but can also be signs of other conditions, she told BBC News.For doctors, symptoms and how someone feels are more useful than appearance.Blood tests matter not only to confirm iron deficiency, Provan and Sesay said, but to establish the cause and guide treatment.Both said treatment should also address the cause. Heavy periods, low dietary iron, gastrointestinal blood loss and problems absorbing iron through the gut can all play a role.Iron deficiency is commonly treated with oral iron. Pavord said iron tablets are best taken on an empty stomach, ideally first thing in the morning, and advised avoiding tea or coffee around the time they are taken because they can inhibit iron absorption.Iron can also be obtained naturally from foods including meat, beans, lentils, leafy green vegetables and fortified cereals.Taking iron supplements without a diagnosis can be harmful, while self-treating could delay the investigation of an underlying problem.Lucy said social media has nevertheless helped women take symptoms more seriously, and has given some the confidence to ask questions when something feels wrong."There are so many women saying, 'Oh my gosh, this is me," she said, adding that she is not a doctor and presents her content as her own experience.For her, doing so has been empowering - giving women information with which to advocate for themselves.Sesay called social media a "double-edged sword" - it can encourage people to seek help, but can also lead them to incorrectly diagnose themselves from a short video.For Lucy, the useful part is not diagnosing yourself from your appearance, but knowing when something doesn't feel right, and when to ask questions.If you'd like to include more iron in your diet, try some of these BBC Food recipes.

schema.headline: Ferritin face: Can you really diagnose low iron from your looks?

title: Trent Alexander-Arnold: Real Madrid defender is struggling for minutes so where does his future lie?
description: Third-choice? Inside Alexander-Arnold's struggles in MadridImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Alexander-Arnold has featured in seven of the 13 m
body: Third-choice? Inside Alexander-Arnold's struggles in MadridImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Alexander-Arnold has featured in seven of the 13 matches Real Madrid have played so far this season, starting four times and registering one assistBySpanish football reporterIt has not been an easy start to the season for Trent Alexander-Arnold.The full-back joined Real Madrid in June 2025 with the ambition of establishing himself as the club's first-choice right-back, but the reality has been very different.The arrival of Denzel Dumfries from Inter Milan this summer added more competition in the position, and now manager Jose Mourinho appears to be favouring Fede Valverde, normally a midfielder, as a starter at right-back.It leaves Alexander-Arnold as third choice and leads to questions on where, and in what role, Mourinho sees the England international's future.Alexander-Arnold has participated in seven of the 13 games Real have played this season, though he has only started four times and has made just one assist - in a 4-0 home win over Malaga.And his involvement has notably declined over the past four games - he did not play against Roma, Sevilla or RB Leipzig and got just a couple of minutes in the Clasico, when he came on in stoppage time.Alexander-Arnold has just turned 28 and Real showed how much they wanted him last summer by paying 10m euros (£8.33m) to secure his early release and make him available for the Club World Cup, rather than wait until he was available on a free transfer when his Liverpool contract expired.But, despite having a contract until 2031, his future now hangs in the balance.'A dream come true'Alexander-Arnold made an excellent first impression at the club, winning over supporters during his first public appearance by delivering his arrival speech in Spanish and saying signing for Real was a "dream come true"."I'm very happy and proud to be here. I'm eager to show the club and the fans what I can do," he added.There was considerable optimism surrounding Alexander-Arnold's arrival, with his signing appearing to form part of the club's succession plan at right-back - he could provide cover for Dani Carvajal while positioning himself as a potential long-term successor to the veteran Spaniard.His first season, however, fell short of expectations.He made 21 La Liga appearances in 2025-26 out of a possible 38, with 14 starts, as injuries and a lack of continuity prevented Alexander-Arnold from establishing himself as a regular presence.For a player arriving with his pedigree and reputation, it was a frustrating start to life in Madrid.There have been several mitigating factors, and Alexander-Arnold is not the only player to have struggled to find his best form during a turbulent period for Real.Firstly, injuries have played a significant role.A hamstring problem in September and a thigh injury in December disrupted his first campaign and denied him the sustained run of games needed to build momentum and develop an understanding with his new team-mates, while a muscle issue during pre-season had already interrupted his preparations.The turnover in management at the club hardly helped either. Xabi Alonso's departure and Alvaro Arbeloa's subsequent appointment meant Alexander-Arnold had to adapt to a change in leadership during his debut season.Neither tenure brought the consistency Real had hoped for, while Mourinho now faces the task of finding the right balance within a squad packed with talent.Could he leave Real Madrid in January?Mourinho has addressed speculation that Alexander-Arnold could leave Real Madrid in January, admitting that difficult selection decisions can be painful but insisting that the team's needs must come first."First of all, it hurts me. I don't like to make players feel bad. I want them to feel good," Mourinho said. "Obviously, when you build a squad with two players per position as your foundation and then have a third player take the field, that's something I don't like."But there are things that are more important than these feelings. Things that are more important for the team at a given moment. And I decided that right now, the move was to change up the midfield and put Fede [Valverde] in there."But I was thinking about the team, not the players. Trent and Dumfries took it well when I explained that it was a decision for the team and not against the players." Mourinho has previously highlighted Alexander-Arnold's versatility and tactical intelligence, insisting that squad rotation and positional flexibility will be crucial to Real's success.Speaking at his first news conference in August, Mourinho stressed that competition for places would be important, naming Trent alongside Netherlands international Dumfries."It is not possible to think that one will play 60 games and the other none," he said, underlining the need to keep his squad involved and motivated.That flexibility was evident against Inter Milan in September, when Mourinho deployed Alexander-Arnold in central midfield alongside Valverde because several midfield options were unavailable through suspension.Mourinho was pleased with the defender's performance, saying he had "interpreted what he needed to really well, tactically" and that he and Valverde had "worked very well at this level".Despite having to make difficult selection decisions, Mourinho has stressed the importance of keeping every member of his squad motivated and ready to contribute."Right now, we are working to make sure all the players are ready at all times, so everyone feels they could be playing and that they are important. That's very important for motivation."A return to Liverpool?Speaking on The Overlap, former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher said he would welcome Alexander-Arnold's return to the Merseyside club."I'd have him back," Carragher said. "He would get a lot of criticism, because I think he made a mistake. I think he made a big mistake going to Madrid."We've definitely missed his creativity."Carragher also highlighted Alexander-Arnold's position in Real's pecking order."At the moment, he's actually third-choice right-back for Real Madrid. They're playing a midfield player [Federico Valverde] at right-back, so even in El Clasico, Denzel Dumfries, the first-choice right-back, comes on as a substitute."So when you're third choice at a club, they're obviously wanting you to move on."For now, Alexander-Arnold  will be hoping for more minutes in their three upcoming games, two league and one Champions League, before the international break. He will also be hoping to retain his place in Thomas Tuchel's next England squad, which is due to be announced on 6 November before the Nations League fixtures against Croatia and Spain. Alexander-Arnold was recalled for September's international window, ending an absence from the squad dating back to June 2025.However, with competition for the right-back position remaining strong, his lack of regular playing time at club level could count against him. Tuchel will therefore have a decision to make over whether to stick with Alexander-Arnold or turn to alternative options.

schema.headline: Trent Alexander-Arnold: Real Madrid defender is struggling for minutes so where does his future lie?

title: South Africa vs Australia: Five takeaways for England after epic series
description: Cummins concerns and weaknesses to target - takeaways from SA-AustraliaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pat Cummins has been Australia captain
body: Cummins concerns and weaknesses to target - takeaways from SA-AustraliaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pat Cummins has been Australia captain since 2021ByMatthew HenryBBC Sport JournalistIf England fans were in any doubt over the difficulty of this winter's trip to South Africa, they should be no more.The superb Proteas completed victory on the final day of their enthralling series against Australia to reaffirm their status as the best side in the world.The contest was packed with subplots, many of which are relevant to England for their upcoming tour and next summer's Ashes series beyond.Cummins endures worst series in years Australia captain Pat Cummins maintained they are still a "really good side" after the defeat.It is undeniable they stand at an intriguing point in their development, however. Knocked off the top of the Test rankings for the first time in two and a half years, they have an ageing bowling attack and a batting line-up caught between generations.And for the first time in his career there is attention on Cummins himself.One third of Australia's iconic pace trio, with Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, he went more than 62 overs without a wicket between the second innings of the first Test and South Africa's second dig in the third. Only once has he finished a series with a worse bowling average than the 53.66 he returned in South Africa.His expected wickets return of 29.6 suggests he bowled better than those figures suggest, but he has only returned a higher mark on that metric once in his past 20 series.Of course, Cummins has plenty of credit in the bank but questions are bound to be raised given his age.Were the 33-year-old not captain, it may have been him under pressure from Scott Boland to play in the third Test.His call to bowl first in Cape Town also proved poor and he was helpless tactically when South Africa's openers attacked on the first morning before correcting things after lunch.England need a spinnerSince Joe Root returned as Test skipper, England have not picked a frontline spinner and have instead favoured a four-man pace attack of Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson.South Africa's victory in the third Test suggests they will need an alternative before long.Off-spinner Simon Harmer, who once considered playing for England before opting for the country of his birth, took 10-120 to bowl the Proteas to victory in Cape Town - the venue of the third Test against England.Newlands is not typically a spinner's surface but it turned big from the third day. The overall average amount of turn throughout the Test (4.35 degrees) was the fourth-highest in Cape Town on record. The Test a place ahead on the list was last year, against Pakistan.Harmer was helped by having left-arm pace bowlers Starc and Marco Jansen creating footholes outside the right-handers' off stump throughout. Starc will not be a factor against England but Jansen will.England's spin issues are longstanding, meaning there is no easy answer.And whether they pick Shoaib Bashir, return to Jack Leach or Mason Crane or hand a debut to Nottinghamshire's Liam Patterson-White – the recent recipient of an England development contract - they will have stiff competition.Since Harmer returned to Test cricket in 2022, no spinner has a better average anywhere in the world.The frailties to exposeIf England do pick a spinner, it will give them a chance to expose one weakness in South Africa's batting order. This could be needed, given the strength of South Africa's bowling attack with Harmer, Jansen and Kagiso Rabada, backed up by Wiaan Mulder.Captain Temba Bavuma was out to off-spin in four out of his five innings against Australia. The exception, the second Test when he made an epic 179 to turn the series on its head, came when Australia left out their premier tweaker Nathan Lyon.Up until the start of 2025, Bavuma averaged 46.85 against spin but since then his record drops to 21.37. That drops to 15.00 against off-spin and 12.16 when such bowlers are coming over the wicket.More broadly and despite victory, South Africa's problems against the short ball were laid bare again in the third Test when seven of their wickets came when playing the hook or pull.It is a problem that has often hampered England but West Indies and Afghanistan are the only sides averaging worse against short balls in Tests over the past four years.Bat carefully, bat longAnother trend to emerge from Australia's visit was the importance of lower-order runs.In their first-Test victory, Australia added 266 runs after the sixth wicket fell in their first innings.In the second Test, South Africa added 315 in the same period while in the second innings of the third Test they added 206 for the last five wickets - something that effectively won them the Test and series.With the ball repeatedly getting soft as innings wore on, wicket-taking became more difficult.Wickets fell once every 60 balls after the ball was 40 overs old in this series, compared to once every 37 balls in England's series against New Zealand earlier in the summer.In recent years, England's lower order have attacked in an attempt to score quick runs. This series showed the benefit of the lower order batting time, sticking around for the top-order batters and stretching out an innings.Find ways to get Renshaw outOne of Australia's positives from their series defeat was the batting of Matt Renshaw.In his first full series since his recall, he was the highest run-scorer at an average of 61.50.With issues to solve elsewhere - most notably at number three where Marnus Labuschagne has gone 49 innings without a Test century and now looks likely to lose his place - Renshaw batted well enough to be given an extended run at the top of the order.His 190 in the first Test came at number five, but 74 in the third as opener suggested Australia's long-running bid to replace David Warner may finally be over.Before the Ashes next summer, England face Australia in the one-off 150th anniversary Test in Melbourne in March.Root's men, under the new leadership of Stephen Fleming, can use that match to test plans to dismiss Renshaw.While the left-hander was born in Yorkshire, he has never played against England. He averages a solid 42.69 in first-class cricket in the County Championship.England will need to locate a weakness by the time the Ashes begins.

schema.headline: South Africa vs Australia: Five takeaways for England after epic series

title: Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport
description: Image caption, The drone activity saw all late evening flights into Jersey cancelled ByChris CraddockJersey communities reporter and Archie FarmerChan
body: Image caption, The drone activity saw all late evening flights into Jersey cancelled ByChris CraddockJersey communities reporter and Archie FarmerChannel IslandsUpdated 45 minutes agoPeople at Jersey Airport have said they are frustrated and angry that "unauthorised drone" activity caused more flight cancellations for a second night in a row.At 20:05 on Saturday Jersey Airport said it was "experiencing disruption.... affecting inbound flights as a result of further drone activity in the vicinity of the airfield".States of Jersey Police are investigating the incidents and officers have appealed to anyone with information about who is responsible to come forward.Insp Rob McCallum said it was believed "two or three" drones had entered the restricted airspace, but they were not thought to be linked to terrorism.Jersey RFC said their team's flight home from Southampton had been cancelled and it would cost the club "thousands and thousands of pounds", including unforeseen hotel costs.Image caption, Pacific Basirwe was waiting for his family to fly in from Heathrow before their flight was cancelled because of the disruptionPacific Basirwe was waiting for his wife and young son to fly in from London Heathrow when he heard the news.He said: "It's annoying, this should be regulated, and the people doing those things should be prosecuted."It's been two days in a row now… If there is no further action, they will keep doing it, which is not good."The Chief Minister of Jersey, Senator Lyndon Farnham, said operating a drone close to an airport was "not a prank or a harmless hobby"."To those responsible, the message is clear: if you are identified, you should expect to face the full consequences of the law."'Utmost seriousness'He added: "The government and our operational partners are treating these incidents with the utmost seriousness. "Police investigations are ongoing and every available avenue is being pursued to identify those responsible. "We are also working closely with UK authorities and specialist agencies to explore additional operational support, enhanced detection capability and counter-drone technology.""Jersey Airport remains safe, and we are determined to do everything necessary both to identify those responsible and to strengthen our capability to prevent this happening again," he continued."The public can be assured that all relevant agencies are working together at pace and that lessons from these incidents will be acted upon swiftly."Our airport is a vital lifeline for the island. We will not tolerate behaviour that jeopardises its safe operation or undermines public confidence in our transport infrastructure."Image caption, Players and staff from Jersey RFC are stuck in the UKJersey RFC said while the team's flight taxied, it returned to the stand and stood there for a few hours before finally being cancelled around 21:30 GMT. A spokesperson said: "As this was a group booking, there was no scope for rebooking given that it is half-term and sufficient flights were not available today. "The team have had to rebook from Southampton on Monday morning. As a community club we have to work incredibly hard to fund local rugby and travel. "Put simply this will cost thousands and thousands of pounds, including unforeseen hotel costs. "Whilst we'll leave the authorities to investigate, the acts of a few have far impacting consequences both financial and physical. It couldn't be further from a 'bit of fun'."Image caption, Richard De La Haye said the last couple of nights have been difficultRichard De La Haye has been a taxi driver for more than 40 years and believes the drone activity is affecting business for drivers like him.He said: "It's a bit of a nightmare because we're sitting here for a couple of hours really not knowing what's going to happen."De La Haye added: "If we pull away and the flights come in then people will be stranded waiting for taxis but if they don't come in we're sat here for two hours waiting for passengers."It's getting silly and I don't know the answer, but it really needs to be resolved, quite honestly."Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to channel.islands@bbc.co.uk, external.

schema.headline: Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport

title: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNardine SaadUS reporterAs Americans prepare to vote in the US midterm elections, candidates with their eye on Congress are not just competing on policy.In our social media age, they're using their personal style to attract attention and project their message. Their clothing has become a measure of their authenticity and appeal."Politicians are dressing for two jobs at once: to look capable of holding office but to also look connected to the people they want to represent," said Joe Zee, a celebrity fashion stylist.From Alaska to Texas, here is a look at how some candidates have been standing out on the campaign trail.Dressing like their stateSome candidates, like Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who represents Washington's 3rd Congressional District, are embracing a relaxed, outdoorsy image.The former car repair shop owner is up for re-election on a platform focused on support for small businesses and working families, after capturing a Republican-held seat in her state in 2022. She favours low fuss, low-key work jackets, flannel shirts, jeans and practical footwear.Robert Ordway, conservative public policy adviser and former owner of Capitol Hill Clothiers, says Gluesenkamp Perez is probably the most "spot-on" when it comes to "authenticity and where you come from"."Also it really vibes with the Pacific Northwest, which has trees and forests and a little bit more of an outdoor vibe," he says.Her style also "shepherds a message championing the working class", says Tashira Halyard, an attorney, content creator, and public policy expert based in Washington DC.Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Gluesenkamp Perez chooses a workwear-inspired wardrobeDemocratic lawmaker Mary Peltola, running for a Senate seat in the battleground state of Alaska, takes a similar approach.She made headlines for wearing traditional boots of the Yup'ik people while being sworn in as a congresswoman in 2022.During this election cycle, her rugged outdoor gear nods to her days working on a fishing boat on Alaska's Kuskokwim River and her "fish, family and freedom" campaign slogan.The flannels, puffer jackets and indigenous-inspired details seem designed to remind voters that Peltola is a native (and Native) Alaskan, says conservative author and journalist Bonnie Kristian.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Mary Peltola wore the traditional footwear of the Yup'ik people when she was sworn inPatriotism on their sleevesOther candidates, such as Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson of Iowa, have been opting for a bolder, patriotic image.While polished and conservative, her style of dress has included classic, arguably nostalgic touches, including denim and bandanas for more casual appearances.In a tight race against her Democratic opponent, Hinson has tried to separate herself from specific policy decisions made by the Trump administration but has still expressed loyalty to the president.She slipped into pumps with the American flag bedazzled across them at a primary election party in Iowa in June. The look, reminiscent of the style worn by Trump supporters at rallies, is quintessential American patriotism, according to Halyard."Ashley's American flag high heels, denim dress and bright red blouse worn with a bandana around her neck are classic Americana," she says."It's this idea that… I'm literally going to wear my patriotism on my sleeve."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Ashley Hinson's campaign style is inspired by the American flag Journalist Bonnie Kristian says there is "a strategic advantage" to Hinson's look, one in which she is "cultivating a visual identity that cannot possibly be misinterpreted" in an era where social media presence, if only for a split second, is crucial."Her denim dress, red bandana and sparkly American flag shoes all signal that she's a Republican wooing rural voters - and indeed she is."Tie off, cowboy boots onOnce a reliable Republican stronghold, Texas has become a battleground between top prosecutor Ken Paxton, 63, who was controversially endorsed by Trump over a longtime senator, and Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico, 37.On the campaign trail, both contenders have been making similar clothing choices, wearing relaxed blazers and cowboy boots.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite political differences, Talarico, left, and Paxton have similar wardrobes"The necktie is dead on the campaign trail in both parties," says Ordway."The younger man dresses up to look serious, and the older man dresses down to look like one of the guys."Fashion critic Friedman notes that Talarico's handcrafted Lucchese cowboy boots "are a very deliberate choice that allows him to speak to all different kinds of constituencies in Texas"."Those boots mean something that is very deeply rooted in Texas semiology," Friedman says, referring to the study of signs and their interpretations. "Former US President George W Bush wore Lucchese cowboy boots, so suddenly you're crossing all sorts of party lines and tapping into all sorts of different electoral groups with your shoes."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Former US president George W Bush was a fan of cowboy bootsMeanwhile, Paxton's style of dress has come under fire on more than one front. It has drawn the disapproval of Trump who has urged voters to focus on his record because it "speaks a lot louder than the suit he's wearing that doesn't look so great".The Republican candidate has also been criticised by his opponent for wearing a pricey watch and polo shirt from the luxury hotel chain Four Seasons as a debate about the high cost of living dominates the midterms."The criticism around his apparent luxury watch and Four Seasons polo raises another style-branded question: casual clothes don't necessarily communicate an ordinary lifestyle," says Zee, a stylist and faculty associate at Arizona State University's Fashion Institute of Design and Merchandising."A five-star resort-branded polo can carry luxury associations just as clearly as a suit. "The watch's identity and value were unconfirmed, but the perception illustrates how an accessory can complicate a candidate's message," he explains.Image source, Facebook/KenPaxtonTXImage caption, Paxton's watch and Four Seasons polo shirt drew criticismPersonal uniformsA uniform, if it reads naturally, is an incredibly effective tool, says Friedman, and a great way to be recognised across the country.It's an approach adopted by Republican Senator and former congresswoman for Tennessee's 7th congressional district, Marsha Blackburn, who is running for governor of her state.Senator Blackburn is often seen in structured jackets and skirts, sometimes with patterns. Ordway remembers that Blackburn "was extremely polished" whenever he spotted her in Capitol Hill while working there as a legislative director for a former Indiana senator."I always saw pearls on her," he says. "Since she's a veteran politician I think how she dresses in relation to how voters see her was probably decided many, many years ago."Image source, BBC NewsImage caption, Marsha Blackburn has been wearing a consistent style for decades"Her looks tend to be fairly timeless - we could imagine GOP women wearing many of them any time in the last three decades," Kristian adds.Meanwhile, Michigan Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, who is in a highly competitive race against a Trump-backed former congressman, has adopted a consistent look of black V-neck T-shirt and blue jeans.The left-wing political outsider, whose campaign slogan is "money out of politics, money in your pocket", refers to his outfit choices as "minimal look, maximal politics". The effect, says Ordway, is reminiscent of a start-up entrepreneur, designed to appeal to an urban, working-class electorate.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdul El-Sayed calls his outfit "minimal look, maximal politics"It also removes much of the "ceremony of a political appearance", Zee says."The suggestion is that attention should go to what he is saying. But the plain T-shirt remains an image choice. Looking un-styled can still be a deliberate form of branding."Trump, master of the imageImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Trump's suit and red tie is instantly recognisableFriedman notes that the master of this look in the US at the moment is Trump. His instantly recognisable power suit and red tie, ever-present in film and reality TV, were cultivated even before he moved into the White House."[Trump] doesn't just have his own merch, but he's got his own outfit, and now he's got all his cabinet wearing the same outfit, and half the Senate is wearing his outfit, and it becomes like a Pavlovian signifier," Friedman says."If they're wearing a navy suit, red tie, and white shirt, you're like, 'oh, that's a Trump person,'" she says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wear similar looksWhatever the outcome of the elections for Trump and his party, Friedman expects to see more politicians effectively branding themselves with their clothing when the 2028 general election rolls in."What we see is that so much of politics now is fought over social media and over TV, and that places a premium on visual messaging that is only going to become more important."

schema.headline: 'The necktie is dead': How US midterm candidates are dressing for votes

title: 'Albinism means you are never invisible', say Coventry siblings
description: Image source, Naseem AkhtarImage caption, All six of the Parvez-Akhtar siblings and their parents, from Coventry, have albinism ByVic MinettBBC Covent
body: Image source, Naseem AkhtarImage caption, All six of the Parvez-Akhtar siblings and their parents, from Coventry, have albinism ByVic MinettBBC Coventry and Warwickshire and Chloe HughesWest MidlandsGrowing up in Coventry, Naseem Akhtar and her family faced judgement because of the way they looked.Although they come from Pakistani heritage, albinism runs in the family - both of her parents, all six of their children, herself, and various other relatives have the genetic condition.Albinism affects the production of melanin, which can affect eyesight as well as they way people with the condition look. This means the family have very pale skin and white hair - something which Akhtar said they faced mistreatment for."I used to hate bonfire night because you knew that the fireworks were going to come through the letterbox," she told the BBC.Growing up in the city in the 80s, Akhtar found it difficult."When I came along, the stigma was a lot more prominent... it would have been more prominent for my father and my mother and my uncle and aunt who had the condition, because they were born in Pakistan... they came to Coventry at about 11 and 12."You're never invisible... you will stand out in any community and that takes a lot of strength and courage to fit in to that and to grow into yourself."Image source, Naseem AkhtarImage caption, Naseem Akhtar said she was bullied as a child and the condition was not accepted"I think that the traumas that we suffer as a child not fitting into your skin, into your identity, I think that then can play out later in life," she said."You have to kind of deal with those feelings... your nervous system got programmed by feeling that feeling of threat because when you were walking around as a child and you were experiencing bullying because you look different."Despite this, Akhtar wanted to raise awareness of the condition from a young age."I was about 11 years old, I went onto the local radio to talk about albinism... I did that because I wanted to change that perception that people had - that we weren't the family that could just be dumped on or to be bullied."Image source, Naseem AkhtarImage caption, Akhtar said by talking about the condition, she hoped she could help the next generations of those with albinismAkhtar is 14 years older than one of her siblings, Mohammed Rafi, now 32, and said the treatment he received growing up was a lot more accepting."We stayed in the same same area in Coventry, so our neighbours, community... they know us that way and there was more awareness over the years," said Rafi.Akhtar added: "And that shows progression, that Rafi's experience is completely different to mine, which I think can only mean that we as a society are more accepting of difference, and we are more integrated a little bit.""The main thing that we struggle with is the vision," added Rafi, who has poor eyesight.The reduced amount of melanin in albinism can cause eye problems, including poor eyesight, astigmatism, or photophobia, according to the NHS, external.Image source, Naseem AkhtarImage caption, The siblings were given a Guinness World Record in 2022In 2022, they received a Guinness World Record for the most siblings with albinism.Akhtar described this as a "mark that that it's OK to be different and and it's all right".None of their children have albinism, but do carry the gene.The siblings said they were not sad that the condition could end in the family in their children's generation."Although we carry this uniqueness, we also know the struggle of how it has been to find our way in life and to live life in this unique way," said Akhtar."Our children will not struggle with the difficulties of having a disability and a long-term condition, I think that's the blessing."Although we have learned to grow into ourselves... it's hard work trying to grow into your skin."'If I inspire others, I've done my bit'Akhtar added that in talking about the condition, she hoped she could help the next generations of those with albinism."We're able to advocate for that, we're able to like have a voice for that and to change that because a lot of it is your perception, the more you change your perception about how you feel about yourself you will have a better life."I was inspired as a child, my specialist teacher that came to support me when I was younger, he had albinism."He inspired me, so if I as a person can give something back to this world - to inspire others - then I feel like I've done my bit on this earth."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Coventry & Warwickshire

schema.headline: 'Albinism means you are never invisible', say Coventry siblings

title: Heidi Klum's Halloween costume revealed as Traitors' Maya Jama dresses as Mo Farah
description: From Maya as Sir Mo Farah to Heidi as her own left hand: The best Halloween looksFigure caption, Watch: Heidi Klum as a giant severed hand for 25th an
body: From Maya as Sir Mo Farah to Heidi as her own left hand: The best Halloween looksFigure caption, Watch: Heidi Klum as a giant severed hand for 25th annual Halloween bashByJacob PhillipsSupermodel and TV host Heidi Klum confirmed her position as the queen of Halloween by transforming into a giant, bloodied and severed hand for her annual costume party in New York.Klum, 53, was completely unrecognisable arriving at her event in what she described as her own chopped-off "left hand".This year marks the 25th anniversary of Klum's party, which brings celebrities across the globe together dressed in their wild, weird and wonderful costumes.And the revelry didn't stop there, with celebrities such as Maya Jama wowing attendees at her own Halloween party in London dressed as four-time Olympic champion Sir Mo Farah.Image source, Getty Images for Heidi KlumImage caption, Klum said her costume this year needed the help of up to 20 people to complete"It took a lot of hands putting this hand together," Klum told reporters as she posed for pictures on the red carpet. "I think about 10 or 20 hands."Explaining the inspiration for the idea, she said: "I looked at my hand and I thought 'Hey, I think that I can fit my body inside of this somehow.'"I always try to come up with something unusual and I don't think I've seen an actual person walking around like a hand. I thought that was something new and different."Klum is never one to shy away from dressing up on the scariest day of the year, with previous looks including a worm, Medusa and the ogre Princess Fiona from the Shrek films.Image source, Getty Images for Heidi Klum HalloweenImage caption, At the party, Klum later lost the full hand costumeOther attendees at Klum's party this year included actors Neil Patrick Harris and David Burtka, who surprised attendees by dressing as the twins from the horror film The Shining.Image source, Getty Images for Heidi KlumImage caption, Harris and his husband Burtka looked eerie in their matching outfitsPop star Jade Thirlwall also attended the party in New York dressed as a stone statue of an angel, while Severance and Spider-Man actor Tramell Tillman turned up with intricate face makeup and prosthetics.Image source, Getty Images for Heidi Klum HalloweenImage caption, Jade transformed herself to look like she was made of stoneImage source, Getty Images for Heidi Klum HalloweenImage caption, Tillman arrived with fake ears and tufts emerging from his foreheadMeanwhile in London, broadcaster Maya Jama hosted her annual Halloween Party dressed as Sir Mo Farah.Jama told Elle UK magazine she wanted to dress as the "bald headed icon" to honour the Olympian, adding that she has wanted to dress up as a man for years for Halloween."[Sir Mo] loved the idea," she explained."He's actually sent me all of his real life Olympic outfits, his real, actual medals he won for the Olympics."His real trainers. He's even done some TikToks for me. He is fully on board."Image source, Getty Images for Maya Jama Annual Halloween PartyImage caption, Jama celebrated Olympic champion Sir Mo FarahImage source, Getty Images for Maya Jama Annual Halloween PartyImage caption, Ryan recreated one of Jama's most talked-about Traitors looks

schema.headline: Heidi Klum's Halloween costume revealed as Traitors' Maya Jama dresses as Mo Farah
